title: Got a meeting? Take a walk
speaker: Nilofer Merchant

keyTerms.definition: a result of something, often a bad one
something you must do, for example for work
to look at a problem in a new way

predictionQuestion: Why might sitting all day be a problem? How could people sit less at work?

keyIdeas.text: We sit so much that we don't question it. She compares sitting to the smoking of our generation.
People sit about 9.3 hours a day, which is more than they sleep (about 7.7 hours).
Sitting too much has serious health consequences.
Examples: some cancers, heart disease and type 2 diabetes.
The health facts didn't change her behaviour. A social invitation did: someone asked her to a meeting while they walked their dogs.
Now she has walking meetings instead of coffee or conference-room meetings, about 20 to 30 miles a week.
She used to think she had to choose between her health and her work.
Lesson 1: getting outside ("out of the box") leads to new, creative thinking.
Lesson 2: problems that seem opposite can often both be solved. Reframe them so both things can be true.
Her final message: walk and talk. Fresh air brings fresh thinking.

modelNotes: - sit ~9.3 hrs/day > sleep (~7.7) → so common we don't question it
- health: some cancers, heart disease, type 2 diabetes
- invite: meeting + walk dogs → now walking meetings (20–30 miles/wk)
- before: health vs work (one OR the other)
- 1. out of the box → out-of-the-box thinking
- 2. 'opposite' problems → reframe → both can be true
End: walk + talk → fresh air = fresh thinking

questions.explanation: Her first lesson: getting out of the box leads to out-of-the-box thinking.

questions.stem: What is her point about health and work?

Health is more important than work

questions.explanation: She used to see health and work as competing, but walking meetings let her do both.
